I have been running onboarding programmes for fourteen years and I want to tell you what the first six months of a job actually look like, as opposed to what the training plan says. People are thrown in at the deep end. That is not a failure of the plan, it is simply what happens, because the plan covers the systems and the policies and it cannot cover the part that matters, which is how this particular room works. So people pick it up. They watch somebody else handle a difficult call and they copy it. Almost nobody is formally taught the thing they end up being good at. Now, here is the part that I think does real damage, and it is about memory rather than training. When people look back on that period, they remember the difficulty very clearly and they forget that they got the hang of it. So the next hard thing arrives and it feels like the first one all over again, as if nothing had been learned. That is why I ask everybody I work with to write down three things they could not do two years ago and can do now. Nobody keeps that list. And without it, every new difficulty looks like evidence that you cannot do difficult things.

A group of psychologists asked more than nineteen thousand people two questions. How much have you changed in the last ten years, in your tastes, your values, your personality. And how much do you expect to change in the next ten. The answers were extraordinarily consistent, and extraordinarily wrong. At every single age, people reported a great deal of change behind them and predicted very little change ahead. Twenty year olds, forty year olds, sixty year olds. Everybody looked back and saw transformation, and looked forward and saw more of the same. And the beautiful thing about the design of the study is that it contains its own refutation. The forty year olds predicted that they would barely change by fifty, and the fifty year olds, right there in the same data, reported that they had changed enormously since forty. The researchers called it the end of history illusion. Everyone feels they have just now become the finished version of themselves. The explanation they offer is almost embarrassingly simple. Remembering is easy and imagining is hard, and people mistake the difficulty of imagining themselves different for evidence that they will stay the same.
